Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verses 1–2:

(p-343) Surat Ibrahim [ʿalayhi as-salam]

It is Meccan, with no disagreement among them that we know of, except for what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah, that they both said: "Apart from two verses within it, namely His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for disbelief﴾ and what follows it [Ibrahim: 28, 29]."

His saying, exalted is He: "Alif-Lam-Ra." Its explanation has already preceded [Yunus: 1]. As for His saying: ﴿A Book﴾, az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: this is a Book, and the Book is the Qur'an.

Regarding what is meant by the "darknesses" and the "light," there are three opinions:

One of them: the darknesses are disbelief, and the light is faith; this was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: the darknesses are misguidance, and the light is guidance; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

(p-344) The third: the darknesses are doubt, and the light is certainty; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Regarding His saying: ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾ there are three opinions:

One of them: by the command of their Lord; this was said by Muqatil. The second: by the enabling (tawfiq) of their Lord; this was said by Abu Sulayman. The third: that it is the permission itself, so the meaning is: by what He has permitted you of teaching them; this was said by az-Zajjaj, who said: Then He clarified what the light is, so He said: ﴿to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is like the Arabs' saying: "I sat with Zayd, with the intelligent, the virtuous," and "ila" (to) is repeated only to magnify the matter. The poet said:

When my leg went numb, I remembered the one who has claim upon it, so I called out to Lubna by her name, and I called out (to her).

I called out to her who, if my soul obeyed me, I would have cast myself from her love and been done (with it).

So he repeated "I called out" to emphasize the matter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "al-Hamid Allah" (in the genitive) as a substitution (badal). Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, Aban, and al-Mufaddal recited "al-Hamid Allahu" with a nominative (raf') as a new sentence (istinaf). The explanation of the wording of the verse has already preceded.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 3–6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who prefer the worldly life over the Hereafter﴾, i.e., they prefer it (yu'thirūnahā) ﴿over the Hereafter﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they take what is hastened for them from it, out of disregard for the matter of the Hereafter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they bar from the path﴾, i.e., they prevent people from entering His religion ﴿and they seek to make it crooked﴾. We have explained this in (Āl ʿImrān: 99).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are in error﴾, i.e., in going astray from the truth ﴿far off﴾ from what is right.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except in the tongue of his people﴾, i.e., in their language. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of "lugha" (language) among the Arabs is speech that is uttered, and it is derived from their saying: "lagha al-ṭāʾir yalghū" (the bird chirped), when it made a sound at the pre-dawn darkness (al-ghalas). Abu Rajaʾ, Abu al-Mutawakkil and al-Jahdari read: "bi-lusuni qawmihi" with a raised lām and sīn, without an alif. Abu al-Jawzāʾ and Abu ʿImran read: "bi-lisni qawmihi" with a kasra on the lām and a sukūn on the sīn, without an alif.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that he may make clear to them﴾, i.e., that with which he was sent, so that they may understand it from him. This was revealed because the Quraysh said: "Why are all the books non-Arabic, while this is Arabic?"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that bring out your people﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "an" (that) is explanatory, and the meaning is: We said to him, "Bring out your people." The explanation of "darknesses" and "light" has already passed [al-Baqara: 257].

(p-346) Regarding His saying: ﴿and remind them of the days of Allah﴾ there are three opinions:

One: that they are the blessings of Allah. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Qutayba said likewise.

The second: that they are the events of Allah among the nations before them. This was said by Ibn Zayd, Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

The third: that they are the days of Allah's blessings upon them and the days of His retribution upon those who disbelieved among the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for every patient one, grateful﴾, meaning: in the reminder ﴿are signs for every patient one﴾ in obedience to Allah and in refraining from His disobedience, ﴿grateful﴾ for His favors. Al-ṣabbār is one who is greatly patient, and al-shakūr is one who is greatly thankful. He specified the signs for them because they benefit from them. What follows this has been explained in Surah (al-Baqara: 49).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 7–14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ is mentioned in (al-A'raf: 167).

Regarding His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ there are three opinions:

One: "If you are grateful for My blessings, I will surely increase you in obedience to Me." This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: "If you are grateful for My bounty, I will surely increase you from My grace." This was said by al-Rabi'.

The third: "If you affirm My oneness, I will surely increase you in good in this world." This was said by Muqatil.

Regarding His saying: ﴿But if you deny﴾ there are two opinions:

One of them: that it is disbelief in tawhid (monotheism). The second: the ingratitude for blessings (kufran al-ni'am).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy﴾ means: He is free of need from His creation, praiseworthy in His actions, because He is either bestowing grace by His action, or He is just.

(p-348) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿None knows them except Allah﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: That is, none counts their number except Him, since Allah destroyed nations from the Arabs and others, so their news was cut off and their traces effaced, and none knows them except Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But they put their hands over their mouths﴾ There are seven opinions regarding it:

One: that they bit their fingers out of rage. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Zayd. Ibn Qutaybah said: "fi" (في, "in") here carries the meaning of "ila" (إلى, "to"), and the meaning of the statement is: they bit upon them in fury and rage, as the poet said:

They return to his mouth the ten [fingers] of the envious one

meaning: they enrage the envious one until he bites on his ten fingers. Similar is the saying of al-Hudhali:

His nails have been consumed by his biting, so he has come to bite upon my wrist-joint (al-wazif)

He says: he has eaten his fingers until he has destroyed them by biting, so he has come to bite upon the wrist-joint of the forearm.

The second: that when the Messenger came to them and said, "Indeed I am a messenger," they would say to him, "Be silent," and would point with their fingers to the mouths of their own selves, rejecting him and denying him. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-349) The third: that when they heard the Book of Allah, they clamored and returned their hands to their mouths. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that they placed their hands over the mouths of the messengers, in rejection of what they said. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: that they denied them with their mouths and rejected their statement. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The sixth: that it is a metaphor, meaning that they refrained from what they were commanded to accept of the truth, and did not believe in it. It is said: "So-and-so returned his hand to his mouth," meaning he held back and did not respond. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

The seventh: they rejected what, had they accepted it, would have been blessings and bounties from Allah; so the word "aydi" (أيدي, "hands") carries the meaning of "ayadi" (أيادي, "bounties"), and "fi" (في, "in") carries the meaning of "ba'" (باء, "with"), and the meaning is: they rejected the bounties with their mouths. This was mentioned by al-Farra', who said: "We have found among the Arabs those who use 'fi' in place of 'ba',' saying: Allah has admitted you 'bi-al-Jannah' (with/into Paradise), meaning 'fi al-Jannah' (in Paradise)." And one of them recited to me:

I am not keen on her concerning Luqayt and his kin, but I am not keen on Sanbas

So he said: "arghabu fiha" (I am keen on her), meaning: a daughter of his, meaning "arghabu biha" (I am keen with her). Sanbas is a tribe.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent"﴾ That is: according to your claim that you were sent, not that they acknowledged their being sent. The remainder of the verse has already been explained (Hud: 62). ﴿Their messengers said, "Is there doubt about Allah?"﴾ This is a rhetorical question of denial, and the meaning is: there is no doubt about Allah, that is, about (p-350) His oneness. ﴿He invites you﴾ through the messengers and the books ﴿to forgive you of your sins﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "min" (مِن, "of") is superfluous, like His saying: ﴿Then there is none of you who could withhold Him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47]. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

I repaid you double the love when you complained of it, and no one before me had repaid you double

meaning: "ahadun" (أحدٌ, "anyone"). His saying: ﴿and delay you until a specified term﴾, which is death; the meaning is: He will not hasten the punishment upon you. ﴿They said﴾ to the messengers, ﴿You are not﴾ meaning: you are not ﴿but human beings like us﴾, that is: you have no superiority over us. "Sultan" means: proof. The messengers said: "We are only human beings like you," and so they acknowledged this to them. ﴿But Allah confers His favor upon whom He wills﴾, meaning: with prophethood and messengership. ﴿And it was not for us to bring you a sultan except by permission of Allah﴾, that is: this is not from ourselves.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He has already guided us to our ways﴾ There are two opinions regarding it:

One: He has made clear to us our right course. The second: He has taught us the way of reliance upon Him. He related this and similar things to our Prophet ﷺ so that he might follow the example of those before him in patience, and so that he might know what befell them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We will surely destroy the wrongdoers﴾ meaning: the disbelievers in the messengers. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿after them﴾, that is: after their destruction. ﴿That﴾ dwelling [in the land] is ﴿for those who fear My standing﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: those who fear His standing before Me. al-Farra' said: The Arabs sometimes attribute their verbs both to themselves and to what they are applied to, saying: "I have regretted my striking you," and "I have regretted your striking," and this is of that type. Similar is ﴿and you make your provision﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82], meaning: My provision to you.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and fears My threat﴾. Ya'qub read "wa'idi" (وعيدي, "My threat") with the ya' in both states, and Warsh followed him in connected recitation.

He replied: "al-wara'" is the name for what is hidden from your eye, whether it is in front of you or behind you. Al-Farra' said: this is only permissible in reference to times such as days, nights, and eras; you say, "Behind you is severe cold" and "Before you is severe cold." It is not permissible to say of a man who is in front of you that he is behind you, nor of a man who is behind you that he is in front of you.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he will be given to drink of purulent water﴾. ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, and the philologists said: al-sadid is pus and blood. Qatadah said: it is what flows from between the skin and flesh of the disbeliever. Al-Qurazi said: it is the wash-water of the people of the Fire, which is what flows from the private parts of fornicators. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is that he is given sadid to drink in place of water. He said: it may also be figurative, meaning: what is given to drink is water as if it were sadid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He gulps it down﴾. Tajarru' means taking a drink sip by sip, not all at once, and this is due to his intense aversion to it, and he is compelled to drink it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he can scarcely swallow it﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: he is not able to swallow it. One says, "sagha li al-shay'" (it went down easily for me) and "asaghtuhu" (I made it go down). Abu Umamah narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "It is brought near to him, and he dislikes it; when it is brought close to him, it scorches his face and the skin of his head falls off; when he drinks it, it cuts his intestines until it comes out from his anus."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And death comes to him from every place﴾, meaning: the anguish of death, its distress and its pain, ﴿from every place﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

The first: from every hair on his body. This was narrated by ʿAta' from Ibn ʿAbbas. Sufyan al-Thawri said: from every vein. Ibn Jurayj said: his soul clings at his throat, so it does not leave through his mouth and he dies, nor does it return to its place and he finds relief.

The second: from every direction, from above him and below him, from his right and left, behind him and in front of him; this was also said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: they are the afflictions that befall the disbeliever in the Fire, which he called death; this was said by al-Akhfash.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Yet he is not dead﴾, meaning: a death by which life is cut off. ﴿And before him is a severe punishment﴾, meaning: after this punishment. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: after the purulent water. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: after abiding eternally in the Fire. "Ghalidh" means severe.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 18:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The parable of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes﴾. Al-Farra' said: He attributed the parable (mathal) to them, whereas the parable is really for their deeds. So the meaning is: the parable of the deeds of those who disbelieved. A similar example is: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾ [al-Zumar 39:60], meaning: you will see their faces. He also made al-'usuf (the violence) a follower of "day" in its i'rab (grammatical case), whereas the violence actually belongs to the wind. This is permissible in two ways:

The first is that although the violence belongs to the wind, the day may be described by it, because the wind occurs within it, so it is permissible to say "a violent day" just as you say "a cold day" and "a hot day."

The other way is that you intend: "on a day of violent wind," and you omit "the wind" because it has been mentioned at the beginning of the speech, as the poet said:

"And the sheen of coats of mail makes our skins laugh, when it is a day whose sun is dark and eclipsed."

He means: an eclipsed sun. It is related from Sibawayh that he said: in this verse there is an ellipsis (idmar), and the meaning is: "And of what We relate to you is the parable of those who disbelieved," then he began, saying: ﴿their deeds are like ashes﴾. Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Ya'mar and al-Jahdari read ﴿on a violent day﴾ without tanwin on "day."

The exegetes said: the meaning of the verse is that everything the polytheists draw near to Allah by is nullified and they gain nothing from it, like the ashes which the wind has scattered, so that it has no power over any of it. Likewise, they have no power over anything in the Hereafter of what they earned in this world, i.e., they do not find its reward. ﴿That is the far-reaching error﴾, i.e., far from salvation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 19–20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered﴾ (alam tara). Regarding it there are two views:

One: its meaning is "Have you not been informed" (alam tukhbar). This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: "Do you not know" (alam ta'lam). This was said by Muqatil and Abu 'Ubayda.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾. The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: that is, He did not create them in vain, but He created them for a great purpose. ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means: He will cause you to die, O assembly of disbelievers, and will create a people other than you who are better than you and more obedient. This is an address to the people of Makkah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾. That is: not unattainable or impossible to achieve.

(p-356) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will come out before Allah all together﴾. Its wording is that of the past tense, but its meaning is the future. The meaning: they will come forth from their graves on the Day of Resurrection, and the follower and the followed will be gathered together. ﴿Then the weak will say﴾, and they are the followers, ﴿to those who were arrogant﴾, and they are the ones who were followed: ﴿Indeed, we were to you followers.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Taba'an" is the plural of "tabi'," and it is said "tabi'" and "taba'," like "ghaib" and "ghayab" (absent). The meaning: we followed you in what you invited us to.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So will you avail us anything against the punishment of Allah?﴾ That is, will you be warding off from us ﴿any portion of the punishment of Allah?﴾ Qatadah said: ﴿If Allah had guided us﴾, that is, if He had guided us in the world, we would have guided you. They mean: Allah led us astray, so we invited you to error. ﴿It is all the same for us whether we show anxiety or endure patiently﴾. Ibn Zayd said: The people of the Fire said to one another: "Come, let us weep and entreat," for the people of Paradise attained Paradise only through their weeping and their entreaty. So they wept and entreated, and when they saw that this did not benefit them, they said: "Come, let us be patient, for the people of Paradise attained Paradise only through patience." So they were patient with a patience the like of which had never been seen, and that did not benefit them either. At that they said: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we show anxiety or endure patiently; we have no place of escape.﴾

Malik ibn Anas narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: They showed anxiety for a hundred years and were patient for a hundred years. Muqatil said: They showed anxiety for five hundred years and were patient for five hundred years.

We have already explained the meaning of "mahis" (place of escape) in the commentary on surah An-Nisa' (4:121).

The statement of the Exalted, ﴿by the leave of their Lord﴾, means: by the command of their Lord. As for His statement, ﴿their greeting therein will be "Peace"﴾, we have already mentioned it in (Surah Yunus: 10).

The statement of the Exalted, ﴿by the leave of their Lord﴾, means: by the command of their Lord. As for His statement, ﴿their greeting therein will be "Peace"﴾, we have already mentioned it in (Surah Yunus: 10).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 24–25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah sets forth an example?﴾ The commentators said: "Have you not considered" with the eye of your heart, so that you know through My informing you how Allah sets forth an example, that is, He presents a comparison. ﴿A good word﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. ﴿Like a good tree﴾ that is, good in its fruit, so He omitted mention of the fruit, relying on what the speech indicates about it.

Regarding this tree there are three opinions:

The first: that it is the date palm. This is in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Anas ibn Malik, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, and others.

The second: that it is a tree in Paradise. It was narrated by Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that it is the believer. Its root is the established fact that he acts upon the earth and his deed reaches the sky. His saying, ﴿yielding its fruit in every season﴾: the believer remembers Allah at every hour of the day. It was narrated by 'Atiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Its root is firm﴾, that is, in the earth; ﴿and its branches are in the sky﴾, that is, its highest part is raised toward the sky. ﴿Its fruit﴾ is its produce. Regarding the phrase "in every season" (ḥīn) here, there are six opinions:

The first: that it is eight months. This was said by 'Ali, peace be upon him.

The second: six months. It was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was said by al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, and Qatadah.

The third: that it is morning and evening. It was narrated by Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that it is a year. It was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: that it is two months. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The sixth: that it is morning, evening, and every hour. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

Whoever said eight months indicated the period of its bearing, both hidden and apparent. Whoever said six months, it is the period of its bearing until the time of its harvest. Whoever said morning and evening indicated the picking of its fruit. Whoever said a year indicated that it bears only once in the year. Whoever said two months indicated the period of its ripeness; Ibn al-Musayyab said: "Its produce does not come except for two months in the palm." Whoever said every hour indicated that its fruit is eaten continually. Qatadah said: its fruit is eaten in winter and summer. Ibn Jarir said: the spathe (ṭalʿ) in winter is part of its produce, and the unripe dates (balaḥ), the half-ripe dates (busr), the soft dates (rutab), and the dried dates (tamr) are in summer.

As for the wisdom in likening faith to the palm tree, it is for several reasons:

The first: it is very firm in its rooting, so the steadiness of faith in the heart of the believer is likened to its steadiness.

The second: it is very high, so the elevation of the believer's deeds is likened to the height of its branches.

The third: its fruit comes in every season, so what the believer gains of the blessing of faith and its reward at every time is likened to its fruit picked in every season, in its various kinds. Thus, whenever the believer says, "There is no god but Allah," it rises to the sky, and then its good and benefit come to him.

The fourth: it is the tree most similar to a human being. Every tree whose top is cut off puts forth branches from its sides, except this one: when its top is cut off, it dries up. Also, it does not bear fruit until it is pollinated. And it is, as is related, a remnant of the clay from which Adam, peace be upon him, was created.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 26:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the likeness of an evil word﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is shirk (associating partners with God).

As for His saying: ﴿like an evil tree﴾, there are five opinions concerning it:

The first: that it is the colocynth (ḥanẓal), narrated by Anas ibn Mālik from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Anas said likewise, as did Mujahid.

The second: that it is the disbeliever. This was related by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-ʿAwfi narrated from him that he said: The disbeliever's deed is not accepted, nor does it ascend to God the Exalted; so it has no firm root in the earth, nor a branch in the heaven.

The third: that it is the dodder (kashūthā), related by al-Ḍaḥḥak from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: that it is a parable, and not a created tree; related by Abu Ẓabyan from Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-361) The fifth: that it is garlic, also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿uprooted﴾ (ijtuththat). Ibn Qutayba said: it was eradicated and cut off. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ijtathatha al-shay' (I uprooted the thing) linguistically is: I took its entire trunk (juththa) in its completeness.

Concerning His saying: ﴿it has no stability﴾ (mā lahā min qarār), there are two opinions:

One: it has no root; it has not driven a vein into the earth.

The second: it has no permanence.

The meaning of likening the disbeliever to this tree is that no righteous deed ascends for the disbeliever, nor any good word, and his saying has no firm root.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 27:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah makes firm those who believe﴾, meaning: He makes them firm upon the truth through the firm word, which is the testimony that there is no god but Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in the worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: the worldly life is the period of life upon the face of the earth, and the Hereafter is the period of questioning in the grave. This meaning was held by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and there are hadiths that support it.

The second: the worldly life is the period of questioning in the grave, and the Hereafter is the questioning on the Day of Resurrection. This meaning was held by Tawus and Qatada. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: this verse was revealed concerning the trial of the grave, the questioning by the two angels, and Allah Exalted's prompting of the believers with the word of truth at the time of questioning, and His making them firm upon the truth. ﴿And Allah leads the wrongdoers astray﴾, meaning: the polytheists; He leads them astray from this word. ﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾, such as guiding the believer and misguiding the disbeliever.

(p. 362) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for ingratitude?﴾ Regarding those referred to, there are seven opinions:

First: They are the two most wicked (al-Afjarān) of Quraysh: the Banu Umayya and the Banu al-Mughira. This was narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib.

Second: They are the hypocrites of Quraysh. Abu al-Tufayl narrated it from ʿAli.

Third: They are the Banu Umayya, the Banu al-Mughira, and the leaders of the people of Badr who led the people of Badr to Badr. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Fourth: They are the people of Makkah. ʿAta' narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Dahhak also said this.

Fifth: They are the polytheists among the people of Badr. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said this.

Sixth: They are those among the disbelievers of Quraysh who were killed at Badr. Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik said this.

Seventh: The verse is general, encompassing all polytheists. al-Hasan said this. The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: Their exchanging the favor of Allah for ingratitude means that Allah bestowed His favor upon them through His Messenger and settled them in His sanctuary (Haram), but they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger and called their people to disbelieve in Him. This is His saying: ﴿And caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾, that is, destruction. Then He explained the abode with His saying: ﴿Hell, which they will burn in﴾, that is, they will endure its heat, ﴿and what an evil place of settlement﴾, that is, what an evil resting place it is.

The lam in ﴿that they may lead [others] astray﴾ is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah, the lam indicating the eventual outcome), and its explanation has already preceded (Yunus, 10:88). Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 31–36:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say to My servants who have believed﴾. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī pronounced the yāʾ of "ʿibādī" with sukūn (silent).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that they establish prayer﴾. Ibn al-Anbārī said: its meaning is: "Say to My servants: (p-364) establish the prayer and spend," "yuqīmū" and "yunfiqū," so both imperatives were omitted and both responses were left out. The poet said:

؎ So what sort of man are you, what sort of man, when it is said in war, "Who will advance?"

He meant: when it is said, "Whoever advances, advance!" It is also possible that the meaning is: "Say to My servants: establish the prayer and spend," and it was turned away from the form of the imperative to the form of the report. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Say to them: let them establish the prayer, and let them spend," and the lām of the imperative was omitted, because "say" indicates it. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-khilāl" is the verbal noun of "khallaltu fulānan khilālan wa-mukhālallatan," and the noun is "al-khullah," which is friendship.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He subjected for you the rivers﴾, i.e., made them submissive, flowing wherever you wish, and you ride upon them wherever you will. ﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon﴾ so that you benefit from them and are illuminated by their light, ﴿constant﴾ in the work of rectifying what they rectify of plants and others, never slackening. The meaning of "dU'ūb" is the passing of a thing in work according to a continuous habit in it. ﴿And He subjected for you the night﴾ so that you may rest in it, a rest for your bodies, ﴿and the day﴾ so that you may benefit by your livelihood. ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked Him﴾. Concerning this there are five sayings:

One of them: the meaning is "of all that which you asked Him for." This was said by al-Ḥasan and ʿIkrimah.

The second: "of all that you asked Him, if you had asked Him." This was said by al-Farrāʾ.

The third: "And He gave you of every thing you asked Him, a thing," so the word "thing" is supplied, like His saying: ﴿and she was given of every thing﴾ [al-Naml: 23], i.e., of everything in her time, something. This was said by al-Akhfash.

The fourth: "of all that you asked Him and that which you did not ask," because you did not ask for the sun or the moon (p-365) nor for many of the blessings with which He began you, so the first was sufficient in place of the second, like His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Naḥl: 81]. This was said by Ibn al-Anbārī.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And keep me and my sons away﴾, i.e., keep me and them away, and the meaning is: make me firm in avoiding their worship. ﴿My Lord, they have led many people astray﴾, meaning the idols, though they are not described as leading astray nor as acting; but when people went astray because of them, it was as if they had led them astray. ﴿So whoever follows me﴾, i.e., in my religion of monotheism, ﴿then he is of me﴾, i.e., he is upon my creed, ﴿and whoever disobeys me — indeed, You are Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Concerning this there are three sayings:

One of them: "and whoever disobeys me and then repents, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful." This was said by al-Suddī.

The second: "and whoever disobeys me in what falls short of shirk." This was said by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

The third: "and whoever disobeys me and disbelieves, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful, that You may accept his repentance and guide him to monotheism." This was said by Muqātil ibn Sulaymān. Ibn al-Anbārī said: it is possible that he supplicated with this before Allah, the Exalted, informed him that He does not forgive shirk, just as he asked forgiveness for his father.

(p-366) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring﴾. There are two views concerning "min" (some of):

The first: it is for partitive meaning (tab'id). This was said by al-Akhfash and al-Farra'.

The second: it is for emphasis (tawkid), and the meaning is: "I have settled my offspring." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in a valley without cultivation﴾, meaning Makkah, where there was neither farmland nor water ﴿near Your Sacred House﴾. It was called "sacred" (muharram) because it is forbidden to violate its sacred things (muharramat) or to treat its sanctity lightly.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿near Your Sacred House﴾, when there was no house there at that time? Ibrahim built it only after a period of time?

The answer has three aspects:

The first: Allah made the place of the House sacred from the time He created the heavens and the earth. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: "near Your House" refers to the house that existed before it was raised in the days of the Flood.

The third: "near Your House" refers to the house which, in Your prior knowledge, was destined to come into being here. Ibn Jarir mentioned these two (the second and third). Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi used to say: The apparent meaning of the speech indicates that this supplication occurred after the House had been built and Makkah had become a town. But the commentators differ from what he said. Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid that Ibrahim set out from al-Sham with his son Isma'il and his mother Hajar, and Jibril was with him, until he came to Makkah, where there were people called the Amaliqa, outside Makkah. The House at that time was a red mound. Ibrahim said to Jibril: "Is it here that I am commanded to place them?" He said: "Yes." So he settled them in a place in the Hijr, and commanded Hajar to make a shelter there. Then he said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring...﴾ the verse. The people of the Hijaz and Abu 'Amr read the yā' in "innī" (inni-ya) as a vowel-lengthened form, "I have settled".

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, that they may establish prayer﴾. There are two views concerning what this lam (of purpose) is connected to:

The first: it is connected to His saying: ﴿and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾. The meaning is: keep them away from idols so that they may establish prayer. This is the view of Muqatil.

The second: it is connected to the word "I have settled". The meaning is: I have settled them near Your House so that they may establish prayer, because the House is the qibla of prayers. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So make hearts from among the people incline towards them﴾. That is, the hearts of a group of people. Ibn al-Anbari said: The heart is referred to as "af'ida" (hearts) because of the closeness of the heart to the fu'ad (inner heart) and its adjacency to it. Imru' al-Qays said:

"She shot me with an arrow that struck the fu'ad on the morning of departure, and I was not avenged."

Another said:

"As if my fu'ad, whenever a rider passes, is the wing of a crow trying to rise to its nest."

Another said:

"Indeed a fu'ad has led me, out of passion, to you, and over the length of love it is patient."

They mean by fu'ad: the heart.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿yahwi ilayhim (incline towards them)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "tahinnu ilayhim" (yearn towards them). Qatada said: "tanza'u ilayhim" (are drawn towards them). Al-Farra' said: "turiduhum" (desire them), as one says: "I saw so-and-so yahwi nahwaka," meaning he desires you. Some read "tahwā ilayhim" meaning "tahwahum" (desire them), like His saying: ﴿radifa lakum﴾ (An-Naml 72), meaning radifakum (followed you). "Ila" here is for emphasis of the speech. Ibn al-Anbari said: "tahwi ilayhim" means descends towards them and plunges down to them.

Concerning the meaning of this inclination there are two views:

The first: it is the inclination towards Hajj, said by most scholars.

The second: it is love of dwelling in Makkah, related by 'Atiyya from Ibn 'Abbas. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "If Ibrahim had said: 'So make the hearts of people incline towards them,' the Jews and Christians would have performed Hajj, but he said: 'from the people.'"

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾. Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: "What we conceal" refers to the grief over parting from Isma'il, and "what we declare" refers to the love for him. The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: he said this when Isma'il had settled in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and he (Ibrahim) was about to leave him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 39–40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Ishmael and Isaac﴾. That is, after old age. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Ishmael was born to him when he was ninety-nine years old, and Isaac was born to him when he was one hundred and twelve years old.

(p-369) His saying, Exalted is He: "Our Lord, and accept my supplication" (wa-taqabbal duʿaʾi). Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, and Hubayrah, on the authority of Hafs from ʿAsim, read: "wa-taqabbal duʿaʾi" with a yaʾ (ي) when connected (in wasl). Al-Bazzi, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, said: he connects and pauses with a yaʾ. Qunbul, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, said: he gives the yaʾ a sound of ishmam (a slight rounding of the vowel) when connected, without articulating it, and pauses on it with an alif. The rest read "duʿaʾ" without a yaʾ in both situations. Abu ʿAli said: pausing and connecting with a yaʾ is the analogical reading, and ishmam is permissible, because the kasrah indicates the yaʾ.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 41:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: He asked forgiveness for his parents while they were both alive, hoping that they would be guided to Islam. It was also said: by "his parents" he meant Adam and Eve.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, al-Nakha'i and al-Zuhri recited: "wa-liwaladayya" (ولِوَلَدَيَّ), meaning Isma'il and Ishaq, which is indicated by their being mentioned before that.

Mujahid recited: "wa-liwalidi" (ولِوالِدِي), in the singular.

Asim al-Jahdari recited: "wa-liwuldi" (ولِوُلْدِي), with a damma on the waw.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur and al-Jawni recited: "wa-liwaladi" (ولِوَلَدِي), with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the dal, in the singular.

﴿The day the reckoning is established﴾: that is, the day the recompense for deeds becomes manifest. It was also said: its meaning is "the day people stand up for the reckoning," so the word "people" was omitted and "the reckoning" was mentioned alone, since the meaning was understood.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَلا تَحْسَبَنَّ اللَّهَ غافِلا عَمّا يَعْمَلُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾ قالَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ: هَذا وعِيدٌ لِلظّالِمِ، وتَعْزِيَةٌ لِلْمَظْلُومِ.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿مُهْطِعِينَ﴾ فِيهِ ثَلاثَةُ أقْوالٍ:

أحَدُها: أنَّ الإهْطاعَ (ihṭāʿ: الإسراع مع شخوص النظر، أو الإسراع عمومًا) هو النَّظَرُ مِن غَيْرِ أنْ يَطْرِفَ النّاظِرُ، رَواهُ العَوْفِيُّ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ، وبِهِ قالَ مُجاهِدٌ، والضَّحّاكُ، وأبُو الضُّحى.

والثّانِي: أنَّهُ الإسْراعُ، قالَهُ الحَسَنُ، وسَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ، وقَتادَةُ، وأبُو عُبَيْدَةَ. وقالَ ابْنُ قُتَيْبَةَ: يُقالُ: أهْطَعَ البَعِيرُ في سَيْرِهِ، واسْتَهْطَعَ: إذا أسْرَعَ.

وَفِي ما أسْرَعُوا إلَيْهِ قَوْلانِ: أحَدُهُما: إلى الدّاعِي، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ. والثّانِي: إلى النّارِ، قالَهُ مُقاتِلٌ.

والثّالِثُ: أنَّ المُهْطِعَ: الَّذِي لا يَرْفَعُ رَأْسَهُ، قالَهُ ابْنُ زَيْدٍ.

وَفِي قَوْلِهِ: ﴿مُقْنِعِي رُءُوسِهِمْ﴾ قَوْلانِ:

أحَدُهُما: رافِعِي رُؤُوسِهِمْ، رَواهُ العَوْفِيُّ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ، وبِهِ قالَ مُجاهِدٌ، وسَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ، وقَتادَةُ، وأبُو عُبَيْدَةَ، وأنْشَدَ أبُو عُبَيْدَةَ:

؎ أنْغَضَ نَحْوِي رَأسَهُ وأقْنَعا كَأنَّما أبْصَرَ شَيْئًا أطْمَعا

He nodded his head toward me and raised it, as if he had seen something that made him covet it.

وَقالَ ابْنُ قُتَيْبَةَ: المُقْنِعُ رَأْسِهِ: الَّذِي رَفَعَهُ وأقْبَلَ بِطَرَفِهِ عَلى ما بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ. وقالَ الزَّجّاجُ: رافِعِي رُؤُوسِهِمْ، مُلْتَصِقَةً بِأعْناقِهِمْ. و﴿مُهْطِعِينَ مُقْنِعِي رُءُوسِهِمْ﴾ نَصْبٌ عَلى الحالِ، المَعْنى: لِيَوْمٍ تَشْخَصُ فِيهِ أبْصارُهم مُهْطِعِينَ.

(p-٣٧١)والثّانِي: ناكِسِي رُؤُوسِهِمْ، حَكاهُ الماوَرْدِيُّ عَنِ المُؤَرِّجِ.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿لا يَرْتَدُّ إلَيْهِمْ طَرْفُهُمْ﴾ أيْ: لا تَرْجِعُ إلَيْهِمْ أبْصارُهم مِن شِدَّةِ النَّظَرِ، فَهي شاخِصَةٌ. قالَ ابْنُ قُتَيْبَةَ: والمَعْنى: أنَّ نَظَرَهم إلى شَيْءٍ واحِدٍ. وقالَ الحَسَنُ: وُجُوهُ النّاسِ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ إلى السَّماءِ، لا يَنْظُرُ أحَدٌ إلى أحَدٍ.

وَفِي مَعْنى الكَلامِ أرْبَعَةُ أقْوالٍ:

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿لا يَرْتَدُّ إلَيْهِمْ طَرْفُهُمْ﴾ أيْ: لا تَرْجِعُ إلَيْهِمْ أبْصارُهم مِن شِدَّةِ النَّظَرِ، فَهي شاخِصَةٌ. قالَ ابْنُ قُتَيْبَةَ: والمَعْنى: أنَّ نَظَرَهم إلى شَيْءٍ واحِدٍ. وقالَ الحَسَنُ: وُجُوهُ النّاسِ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ إلى السَّماءِ، لا يَنْظُرُ أحَدٌ إلى أحَدٍ.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَأفْئِدَتُهم هَواءٌ﴾ الأفْئِدَةُ: مَساكِنُ القُلُوبِ.

وَفِي مَعْنى الكَلامِ أرْبَعَةُ أقْوالٍ:

أحَدُها: أنَّ القُلُوبَ خَرَجَتْ مِن مَواضِعِها فَصارَتْ في الحَناجِرِ، رَواهُ عَطاءٌ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ. وقالَ قَتادَةُ: خَرَجَتْ مِن صُدُورِهِمْ فَنَشِبَتْ في حُلُوقِهِمْ، فَأفْئِدَتُهم هَواءٌ لَيْسَ فِيها شَيْءٌ.

والثّانِي: وأفْئِدَتُهم لَيْسَ فِيها شَيْءٌ مِنَ الخَيْرِ، فَهي كالخَرِبَةِ، رَواهُ العَوْفِيُّ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ.

والثّالِثُ: وأفْئِدَتُهم مُنْخَرِقَةٌ لا تَعِي شَيْئًا، قالَهُ مُرَّةُ بْنُ شُراحْبِيلَ. وقالَ الزَّجّاجُ: مُتَخَرَّقَةٌ لا تَعِي شَيْئًا مِنَ الخَوْفِ.

؎ ألا أبْلِغْ أبا سُفْيانَ عَنِّي ∗∗∗ فَأنْتَ مُجَوَّفٌ نَخِبٌ هَواءُ

Let it be conveyed to Abu Sufyan from me: you are hollow, feeble-hearted, and empty air.

فَعَلى هَذا يَكُونُ المَعْنى: أنَّ قُلُوبَهم خَلَتْ عَنِ العُقُولِ، لِما رَأوْا مِنَ الهَوْلِ. والعَرَبُ تُسَمِّي كُلَّ أجْوَفَ خاوٍ: هَواءً. قالَ ابْنُ قُتَيْبَةَ: ويُقالُ أفْئِدَتُهم مَنخُوبَةٌ مِنَ الخَوْفِ والجُبْنِ.

(p-372) His words, exalted is He: ﴿And warn mankind﴾, that is, make them fear, ﴿the Day when the punishment comes upon them﴾. By this he means the Day of Resurrection. He specifically mentioned the punishment, although there is also reward in it, because the speech came in the manner of a threat to the disobedient. Ibn ʿAbbas said: By "mankind" here he means the people of Makkah.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then those who did wrong will say﴾, that is, those who associated partners with Allah, ﴿"Our Lord, delay us for a short term"﴾, that is, grant us a brief period of respite. Muqatil said: They asked to be returned to the worldly life, because departure from the world is near. ﴿We will answer Your call﴾, meaning: the Tawhid (Oneness of Allah), so it will be said to them: ﴿Did you not swear before [that there would be] no cessation for you?﴾, that is, you swore in the world that you would not be resurrected and would not pass from this world to the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 45:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, meaning: you settled in their places and their towns, such as al-Hijr (the land of Thamud) and Madyan, and the towns whose people were punished. The meaning of ﴿wronged themselves﴾ is: they harmed themselves through disbelief and disobedience. ﴿And it became clear to you﴾: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read it as "wa-tubayyana" with a ḍammah on the tā'. ﴿How We dealt with them﴾, meaning: how We punished them. He says: it was necessary for you to refrain from opposition, taking heed from their dwellings, after you had come to know what We did to them. ﴿And We set forth for you the examples﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the examples that are in the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 46–47:

(p-373) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they had planned their plan﴾. Regarding those referred to, there are four opinions.

The first: that it is Nimrod, who disputed with Abraham about his Lord. He said: "I will not stop until I look at the sky." So he ordered two young eagles to be raised until they became fat and strong. Then he ordered a chest (tabut) to be carved, and placed in its middle a piece of wood, and on the top of the wood he placed very red meat. He then starved the two eagles and tied their feet with cords to the legs of the chest. He entered it himself with a companion of his and closed its door. Then he released them, and they began to seek the meat, and they rose into the sky for as long as God willed. Then he said to his companion: "Open and look, what do you see?" So he opened and said: "I see the earth as if it were smoke." He said to him: "Close." Then they rose for as long as God willed. Then he said: "Open and look." So he opened and said: "I see nothing but the sky, and we are only increasing in distance from it." He said: "Then straighten your wood." So he straightened it, and the eagles swooped down seeking the meat, and the mountains heard their crash and nearly were displaced from their places. This is the saying of Ali ibn Abi Talib. In another narration from him: the eagles were four. Al-Suddi related from his shaykhs that he kept ascending until he saw the earth surrounded by a sea, as if it were a disc in water. Then he ascended until he fell into darkness, so he could see neither what was above him nor what was below him, and he was terrified. So he straightened the meat, and the eagles swooped down. When he descended, he began building the palace (sarh). Then he ascended from it with the eagles, and when he could not reach the sky, he took it as a fortress, and God brought his building down from its foundations. Ikrimah said: there was with him in the chest a boy who carried a bow and arrows; he shot an arrow, and it returned to him stained with blood. So he said: "The god of the sky has been dealt with," and that was from the blood of a fish in a sea suspended in the air. When the height frightened him, (p-374) he said to his companion: "Straighten the wood." So he straightened it, and the eagles descended, and the mountains thought that a command had come down from the sky, so they moved from their places. Others said: when the mountains saw that, they thought it was the Hour of Resurrection, and they nearly moved. To this meaning went Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik.

The second opinion: that it is Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar), and that this story happened to him; and when the eagles rose seeking the meat to where God willed, he was called: "O tyrant, where do you want to go?" So he was terrified, then he heard the voice above him, and he descended. When the mountains saw that, they thought it was the Hour of Resurrection and nearly moved. This is the saying of Mujahid.

The third: that those referred to are the earlier nations. Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah said: "Their plan" means their shirk.

The fourth: that they are those who plotted against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when they intended to kill him and expel him.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And with God is their plan﴾, there are two opinions:

One: that it is preserved with Him until He repays them for it; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: "And with God is the recompense of their plan."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And though their plan was such﴾. Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, and Abu al-'Aliyah read: "And though their plan almost" (kāda) with the letter dal. ﴿That the mountains would be moved thereby﴾. Most readers read "li-tazūla" with a kasra on the first lam of "li-tazūla" and a fatha on the second. The meaning intended: "and their plan was not such that the mountains would be moved by it," i.e., it is weaker and feebler; this is how al-Hasan al-Basri explained it. Al-Kisa'i read "la-tazūlu" with a fatha on the first lam and a damma on the second, meaning: "the mountains had almost been moved by their plan"; this is how Ibn al-Anbari explained it.

Regarding what is meant by the mountains, there are two opinions:

One: that they are the well-known mountains; this was said by the majority.

The second: that they were presented as a parable for the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the firmness of his religion, like the firmness of the fixed mountains (p-375). The meaning: even if their scheming reached the removal of mountains, the affair of Islam would not be removed; this was said by al-Zajjaj. Abu Ali said: what confirms the soundness of this is His saying: ﴿So do not think that God would break His promise to His messengers﴾, i.e., He has promised you dominance over them. Ibn Abbas said: by His promise he means victory, conquest, and the manifestation of the religion. ﴿Indeed, God is Exalted in Might﴾, i.e., invincible, ﴿Owner of retribution﴾ against the disbelievers, which is that He will repay them with punishment for their disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 48:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the day when the earth will be changed to another earth﴾. Aban narrated "on the day We change" with the nūn (we) and a kasra on the dāl, "the earth" in the accusative, and "the heavens" in the genitive (with a kasra on the tā'). There is no disagreement regarding the accusative of "ghayr" (other than).

Regarding the meaning of the change of the earth there are two opinions:

The first: it is that same earth, but it will be increased in some places and decreased in others, its hills, valleys, rivers and trees will disappear, and it will be stretched out like a hide. Abu Salih narrated this meaning from Ibn ʿAbbas. Abu Hurayrah also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning "the day the earth will be changed to another earth" that he said: "He will spread it out and stretch it like a hide."

The second: it will be replaced by something other than itself. Then there are four opinions on this: First, it will be replaced by another earth, white like silver, on which no sin has been committed; this was narrated by ʿAmr ibn Maymun from Ibn Masʿud, and by ʿAta' from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid also said this. Second, it will be replaced by fire; this was said by Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. Third, it will be replaced by an earth of silver; this was said by Anas ibn Malik. Fourth, it will be replaced by a white loaf, so that the believer will eat from beneath his feet; this was said by Abu Hurayrah, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and al-Qurazi. Others said: the people of Islam will eat from it until their reckoning is finished.

As for the change of the heavens, there are six opinions on it: First, they will be made of gold; this was said by ʿAli, peace be upon him. Second, they will become gardens; this was said by Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. Third, their change is the folding up of their suns and the scattering of their stars; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Fourth, their change is the variation of their states: at one time they will be like molten brass, and at another time like red leather; this was said by Ibn al-Anbari. Fifth, their change is that they will be rolled up like the folding of a scroll for a book. Sixth, they will be split open so that they cast no shade; both of these were mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will come forth before Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾. That is, they will come out of their graves.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verses 49–51:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you see the criminals﴾, meaning the disbelievers, ﴿bound together﴾. It is said: "I joined (qaranta) one thing to another (qarantu al-shay' ila al-shay')" when you connect it to that thing.

(p-377) Regarding the meaning of "muqarranin" (bound together) there are three views:

The first: they are bound together with the devils. This is the view of Ibn Abbas. The second: their hands and feet are bound up to their necks. This is the view of Ibn Zayd. The third: some of them are bound to others. This is the view of Ibn Qutayba.

Regarding "al-asfad" (the shackles) there are three views:

The first: they are the shackles (al-aghlal). This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd, Abu Ubayda, Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari. The second: they are the fetters and shackles. This is the view of Qatada. The third: they are the fetters. This is the view of Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

As for "al-sarabil" (garments), Abu Ubayda said: they are shirts, the singular being "sirbal." Al-Zajjaj said: "al-sirbal" is anything that is worn.

Regarding "al-qatiran" (tar), there are three dialectal readings: the qaf vowelled with a fatha and the ta' with a kasra (qatiran), the qaf with a fatha and the ta' sukun (qatran), and the qaf with a kasra and the ta' sukun (qitran).

Regarding its meaning there are two views:

The first: it is molten copper. Ibn Abi Talha narrated this from Ibn Abbas.

The second: it is the tar of camels. This is the view of al-Hasan, and it is a substance that exudes from a tree with which camels are treated for mange. Al-Zajjaj said: tar was assigned to them because it intensifies the blazing of the fire on the skins. Had Allah, Exalted is He, wished to intensify their burning by other means, He would have been able to do so, but He warned them with something whose reality they know.

Ibn Abbas, Abu Razin, Abu Mijlaz, Ikrima, Qatada, Ibn Abi Abla and Abu Hatim, from Ya'qub, recited "min qitrin" with a kasra on the qaf, a sukun on the ta', and tanwin, and "anin" with a hamza that is cut (qat'), with a fatha on it, and with the alif lengthened (madd). Al-qitr is copper, and "anin" means that its heat has reached its limit.

(p-378) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Fire covers their faces﴾, meaning it rises over them. The lam in "li-yajziya" (so that He may recompense) is connected to His saying: ﴿and they come forth﴾.

Ibn Abbas, Abu Razin, Abu Mijlaz, Ikrima, Qatada, Ibn Abi Abla and Abu Hatim, from Ya'qub, recited "min qitrin" with a kasra on the qaf, a sukun on the ta', and tanwin, and "anin" with a hamza that is cut (qat'), with a fatha on it, and with the alif lengthened (madd). Al-qitr is copper, and "anin" means that its heat has reached its limit.

(p-378) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Fire covers their faces﴾, meaning it rises over them. The lam in "li-yajziya" (so that He may recompense) is connected to His saying: ﴿and they come forth﴾.

This is the commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 14, verse 52:

Allah's words: ﴿This is a message (balagh) for mankind﴾. Regarding what is referred to by "this," there are two opinions:

The first: it is the Qur'an. The second: it is the warning (al-infar). And balagh means sufficiency. Muqatil said: by "mankind" is meant the people of Makkah.

Allah's words: ﴿and that they may be warned thereby﴾. That is: it was sent down so that they may be warned by it, and so that they may know, through the proofs (hujaj) it contains, that He is only one God, and so that ﴿those of understanding may take heed﴾; that is, so that they may be admonished.
